gap: No result ChatGPT got says that BLUETTI's own 350 W panel is rated 33 V open-circuit and the Elite 200 V2 accepts only 12–60 V at 20 A. Two of those panels in series give 66 V, which is too high, so they must be wired in parallel, and then the station can take in at most 20 A × 33 V = 660 W from the 700 W pair. Two SP200L panels in series give 49.2 V and 10.8 A, which fits.
standout_why: ChatGPT's search returned no results, so I had no rival pages to read. I compared against ChatGPT's two answers. They have generic size tables (400–800 W or 800–1,500 W of panels for a weekend cabin) and a calculator (2.2 kWh/day needs a 1.0 kW array and 5 kWh of battery), and they mention 'compatible MPPT' in general terms. Neither answer names a product's solar-input voltage or current window, says how to wire panels to a given station, or warns that one maker's bundled 700 W panel pair can't reach full power on its own station. I scored it 2 rather than 3 because the 660 W figure is a ceiling worked out from Voc, not a measured harvest. BLUETTI's 350 W panel page does not list Vmp, Imp or Isc.
kit_items: Power station / battery: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (2,073.6 Wh LiFePO4 per the page title, 2,600 W AC continuous). Solar input is 12–60 V, 20 A, 1,000 W max, so the panels must fit inside that window.

Solar panels: 2× BLUETTI SP200L 200 W, wired in series. Each panel is 24.6 V Voc and 10.8 A Isc. In series that is 49.2 V and 10.8 A, which is under the 60 V and 20 A limits, so the full 400 W can reach the station. Three in series would be 73.8 V, which is too high.

Avoid for this station, or plan on clipping: 2× BLUETTI 350 W panels. At 33 V Voc each, two in series are 66 V, over the 60 V limit. In parallel, the 20 A limit caps input at 660 W or less from 700 W of panels.

Solar cable: BLUETTI 20 A MC4-to-XT60 cable (Dealectric slug bluetti-solar-charging-cable-mc4-xt60-20a), matched to the station's 20 A input. The 350 W panel ships with this cable; I did not confirm whether the SP200L bundle does.

Scale-up option for a full-time cabin: Sun Gold Power SGR-8K10E. Its maker's listing gives 8× 450 W panels (3.6 kW), an 8,000 W 48 V inverter with dual MPPT and up to 11,000 W of PV input, and 10.24 kWh of LiFePO4 (2× SG48100P 51.2 V 100 Ah), rated at about 14.4 kWh/day of solar over 4 sun-hours.

findings.note: From the product page FAQ (PV input). AC input is 1,800 W max.

findings.label: Battery capacity / AC output
findings.value: 2,073.6 Wh LiFePO4 (headline says 2,080 Wh); 2,600 W continuous
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Portable Power Station | 2,600W 2,080Wh
findings.note: Against ChatGPT's own example load of 2.2 kWh/day: 2,073.6 / 2,200 = 0.94 days of autonomy, so the battery won't cover a full day of that load, let alone ChatGPT's 1.5-day target. This kit fits a weekend cabin using about 1 kWh/day or less.

findings.label: Open-circuit voltage
findings.note: 2 in series = 66 V, over the Elite 200 V2's 60 V maximum, so the pair must go in parallel. In parallel the array voltage is no higher than 33 V and the current is capped at 20 A, so input is at most 33 × 20 = 660 W from 700 W of panels. The real ceiling is lower because Vmp is below Voc. Ships with a 20 A MC4-to-XT60 cable. Price $649.

findings.label: Voc / Isc
findings.note: 2 in series = 49.2 V and 10.8 A, within 60 V and 20 A, leaving 10.8 V of headroom for the voltage rise in cold weather. 3 in series = 73.8 V, which is too high. Rated operating range is -25 to 65 °C. Price $399, or $798 for two.

findings.label: Daily solar refill at ChatGPT's own assumptions
findings.note: 400 W × 3 peak-sun-hours × 0.80 system efficiency (the assumptions ChatGPT stated) = 960 Wh. That refills 2,073.6 Wh from empty in about 2.2 sunny days. ChatGPT's 2.2 kWh/day example would need 2,200 / (3 × 0.8) = 917 W of panels, which is under the station's 1,000 W cap, but only if they can be wired inside the 60 V / 20 A window.

Sun Gold Power SPH8048P inverter MPPT voltage range, max PV Voc and per-MPPT current, and SGN-450 panel Voc/Vmp/Isc: the maker's kit page, retailer pages (offgridstores, offgridsource, outboundpower, renewableoutdoors) and the manual and datasheet PDFs all returned HTTP 429/403, or the PDFs couldn't be parsed here. Search snippets suggested 125–425 V MPPT, 500 V Voc, 22 A per MPPT and a 35.03 V / 30.08 V Vmp panel. If true, two 4-panel strings (about 120 V Vmp) would fall below the MPPT window. That is not opened or verified, so I left it out of findings.
